The load balancer itself secretly forwards state between the two servers
It only works because both requests happen to reuse the same TCP connection

items.prompt: A route is defined as `GET /delete-account`. What's actually wrong with this, given that GET requests work fine over HTTP?
choices: Nothing at all — GET can legitimately trigger any server-side effect the code wants
It violates GET's convention of "no side effects expected," which browsers/proxies may rely on (e.g. prefetching or retrying GETs freely)
GET requests are technically incapable of reaching any server-side handler
The path must always start with /api for any DELETE-like action to work
items.explanation: Methods encode intent by convention, not by network enforcement. Browsers, proxies, and crawlers treat GET as safe to prefetch or retry — a GET route with real side effects can get triggered accidentally by exactly that assumption.
items.reference:
GET

fetch, no side effects expected

POST

create / submit, side effects expected

Why: the method states intent by convention — the network doesn't enforce it, the server's code has to actually honor it.
items.learnMore:
Methods are a convention, not a network rule

Nothing in TCP stops a GET handler from deleting data — the server's own code has to respect the convention.

MethodIntended for
GETFetch, no side effects
POSTCreate / submit
PUT / PATCHReplace / update
DELETERemove

Common mistake

Assuming a method's semantics are enforced by the protocol. A `GET /delete-everything` route is bad practice, not a network error — proxies and browsers that prefetch/retry GETs assuming safety will happily trigger it.

PUT can only ever be used specifically for uploading files

choices: nc has a built-in HTTP client that browsers also secretly rely on
HTTP is just text sent over a TCP connection — nc can send that text manually, same as any HTTP client would
This trick only works for HTTPS traffic, never plain unencrypted HTTP
Web servers grant netcat sessions special elevated permissions
items.explanation: There's no hidden binary layer — HTTP messages are plain text over a TCP connection, so anything that can open a TCP connection and write text to it (nc, a browser, curl) can speak HTTP.
items.reference:
📄 A request is text — readable in a terminal, no binary framing
🔌 Sent over TCP — same transport curl, browsers, and `nc` all use

Why: there's no hidden binary protocol underneath — what you see in `curl -v` is genuinely the whole message.
items.learnMore:
HTTP has no magic underneath it

A browser, curl, and a raw `nc` connection are all doing the same thing at the wire level.

ToolWhat it sends
BrowserPlain HTTP text, built for you

Thinking HTTPS changes this. TLS encrypts the bytes on the wire, but the HTTP message itself is still the exact same readable text underneath the encryption.

items.prompt: A hand-crafted raw HTTP request is missing the blank line between its headers and its body. What actually goes wrong?
choices: Nothing goes wrong — servers simply ignore blank lines entirely
The parser can't tell where headers end and the body begins, since the blank line is the only separator
The request gets automatically rejected outright with a 301 response
The body ends up getting sent as an extra header line instead
items.explanation: The blank line (\r\n\r\n) is the field separator between headers and body — without it, a parser has no signal that headers are finished, and will typically keep treating incoming bytes as more header lines.
items.reference:
GET /x HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
<blank line>
(body, if any)

Why: the blank line is the only signal that tells a parser "headers are done, body starts here."
items.learnMore:
The blank line is a field separator, not decoration

Without it, a parser has no way to know where headers end and the body begins.

SequenceMeaning
End of one header line
End of all headers — body starts right after

Common mistake

Hand-building raw requests/responses and forgetting the final blank line — a compliant parser will keep waiting for more header lines that never come.

items.prompt: Why does HTTP/1.1 keep-alive make writing a request parser harder than assuming one request per connection?
choices: Because keep-alive requests are written using a slightly different text format
The parser must re-synchronize on request boundaries itself, since the connection no longer closes to mark where one request ends
Because a request sent under keep-alive can never include a body
Because keep-alive is only ever used for responses, never for requests
items.explanation: Without a close to rely on, the parser has to track exactly how many bytes belonged to the current request (via Content-Length or chunked encoding) and treat anything after that as the start of the next one.

keep-alive

Why: without a close to rely on, the parser is the only thing that knows where one request ends and the next begins.

items.prompt: A proxy automatically retries a failed `DELETE /articles/42` request, assuming DELETE is idempotent. The server's handler, written poorly, deletes the *next* article in the table each time it's called instead of checking if 42 already exists. What does this expose about idempotency?
choices: Idempotency is guaranteed by the network layer, so a bug like this can't actually happen
Idempotency is only a convention the handler's code has to honor — nothing in HTTP forces DELETE to behave idempotently
DELETE requests are therefore never safe to retry under any circumstance
This specific scenario is a bug in the proxy itself, not in the handler
items.explanation: The DELETE method is supposed to be idempotent by convention, which is exactly why proxies/retry logic feel safe resending it — but that safety only holds if the server's actual implementation honors the convention, which this one doesn't.
items.reference:
📜 The convention — GET/PUT/DELETE, called twice, should have the same effect as once
⚠️ Not enforced — a badly written handler can still make a GET destructive

Why: the convention exists so retry logic can safely resend idempotent methods — but it only holds if the handler actually honors it.
items.learnMore:
Idempotency is a promise, not a guarantee

It's a contract the handler's author has to uphold — nothing in HTTP or TCP enforces it.

MethodSupposed to be idempotent?
GETYes
PUTYes
DELETEYes
POSTNo — repeating it may create a duplicate

Common mistake

Assuming a retry library is always safe to auto-retry any request. It's only safe for methods the handler actually implemented idempotently — retrying a broken POST-as-side-effect handler can double the effect.

items.prompt: Why is it specifically safe, by convention, for a browser or HTTP client to automatically retry a failed GET request, but not a failed POST request?

There's no real difference at all — both are equally safe to retry blindly

items.prompt: TCP delivers a raw stream of bytes with no built-in concept of "message boundaries." Given that, what problem does the `Content-Length` header actually solve?
choices: It compresses the body's bytes in order to save network bandwidth
It tells the receiver exactly how many bytes to read as the body, since TCP alone gives no way to know where the body ends
It verifies cryptographically that the body hasn't been corrupted in transit
It's purely informational metadata with no actual effect on parsing
items.explanation: TCP is just a byte stream — without an explicit length (or chunked encoding), the receiver has no way to know when the body is finished versus when more bytes are still coming.
items.reference:
🌊 TCP — a byte stream, no built-in message boundaries
📏 Content-Length — HTTP's explicit "read exactly this many bytes" instruction

Why: TCP alone can't tell a reader where a message ends — HTTP has to say so explicitly.
items.learnMore:
Two ways to mark where a body ends

Both exist because a receiver has no other way to know when to stop reading.

MechanismWhen it's used
Content-LengthThe full body size is known upfront
Transfer-Encoding: chunkedThe body is streamed and its total size isn't known yet

Common mistake

Computing Content-Length from a string's character count instead of its actual byte count — wrong for any body with multi-byte UTF-8 characters (see L3).

items.prompt: A server wants to stream a response body whose total size isn't known in advance (e.g. a live-generated report). Since it can't supply an accurate `Content-Length` upfront, what's the alternative that still lets the receiver know where the body ends?
choices: Omit any length information entirely, and let the receiver just guess at it
Transfer-Encoding: chunked, which marks the end of the body explicitly without needing the total size upfront
Always close the underlying TCP connection immediately after sending headers
Send the entire body twice over, so the receiver can compare the copies
items.explanation: Chunked encoding sends the body in labeled, self-describing chunks and a final zero-length chunk to mark the end — it solves the same "where does this end" problem as Content-Length, but without requiring the full size to be known in advance.

items.prompt: A monitoring check only verifies that a health endpoint returns `200 OK`. A bug causes the endpoint to always return 200 with an empty body, even when the underlying service has crashed. What does this expose about status codes?
choices: This scenario is impossible — a 200 always means the request succeeded correctly
A status code is a claim the server makes, not a guaranteed fact about the body's correctness — checking only the code, never the body, can miss a real outage
Empty response bodies get automatically converted into a 5xx by the server
The real bug here lies in the monitoring tool's HTTP library, not the check's design
items.explanation: Nothing enforces that a 200's body is actually correct — the status line and the body are set independently by the server's code. A monitoring check that only reads the status code is trusting the server's word for it, and this scenario is exactly where that trust fails.
items.reference:
Status-only check

200 OK, empty body → looks fine, isn't

Status + body check

200 OK, but body shape is wrong → caught

Why: a status code is whatever the server chose to send — trusting it blindly means trusting the server's word for it.

Writing client code (or health checks) that only branches on `response.status`, without ever validating that the body actually matches what a healthy response should look like.

items.prompt: A team adds an in-memory cache on each server instance that stores "the last thing this user did," and now users get inconsistent behavior depending on which server handles their next request. What architectural property did this break?
choices: TLS certificate termination at the load balancer
Statelessness — request handling started depending on server-local memory instead of being fully determined by the request itself
The meaning and behavior of the Content-Length header
The agreed-upon semantics of the HTTP methods themselves
items.explanation: As soon as a server needs its own memory of a prior request to answer correctly, requests are no longer interchangeable across servers — which is exactly the property a load balancer relies on to route freely.
items.reference:
⚖️ Load balancing — any server can take any request
🗄️ Caching — same request always deserves the same cached response

Why: both only work because the request alone determines the response, with nothing left implicit on the server side.
items.learnMore:
Statelessness is an architecture decision, not just a trivia fact

It's the property that lets infrastructure treat servers as interchangeable.

CapabilityRequires
Round-robin load balancingNo server-side memory of prior requests
Response cachingRequest alone determines the response

Common mistake

Adding in-memory server-side session state "just for this one feature," which quietly breaks load balancer interchangeability until sticky sessions are bolted back on.

Because GET requests are specifically exempt from caching rules by convention
Because the CDN silently authenticates itself as the origin server each time
items.explanation: Caching relies on the same statelessness property as load balancing: if the response is fully determined by the request, a cached response is valid for anyone who sends that same request — no per-user memory required.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three parts every HTTP message has?

Headers
An optional body

items.prompt: A raw request is sent with a request line and a body, but zero header lines at all (not even Host). Structurally, is this still the same three-part shape?
choices: No — the shape is still request line + headers (possibly empty) + body; omitting Host doesn't remove the "headers" part of the shape, it just leaves it empty
Yes, but only because headers aren't really part of the shape
No, because a body always requires at least one header

items.prompt: Why does a response's status line carry a "reason phrase" (like "OK" or "Not Found") in addition to the numeric status code?

The reason phrase changes what the numeric code means
It's a legally required piece of text

It's missing headers

items.prompt: You're given a raw byte dump sent over a TCP connection: a line that looks like a status line, followed by headers, followed by a body — but a bug report labels it a "request." What's actually wrong with that label?

A status line (version + code + reason) only ever appears in a response — the first line's *job*, not its presence, is what distinguishes a request from a response, so this is mislabeled; it's a response
This is a valid request variant used specifically for redirects

items.prompt: A client sends the same `PUT /articles/42` request three times in a row because of a flaky network retry. Why is this generally considered safe, by convention?
choices: PUT is meant to be idempotent — replacing a resource with the same data three times should leave it in the same end state as doing it once
PUT always creates three separate copies of the resource
PUT is never safe to retry under any circumstance
PUT and POST carry the exact same intent
items.explanation: Idempotency is exactly the convention that makes blind retries of PUT reasonable — repeating it shouldn't change the outcome.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees `POST /users/42/activate` and doesn't insist on `PATCH` instead. Why might POST be the reasonable choice here?
choices: POST is a reasonable fit when the action is more like "trigger an event" than "replace a resource's stored state"
POST is always wrong for anything except creating brand-new resources
The HTTP spec requires PATCH for every update, no exceptions
There's never a meaningful difference between the two
items.explanation: Methods encode intent, and "activate this account" reads more like triggering an action than replacing a resource's full state — POST fits that intent fine.

items.prompt: Two endpoints, `GET /search?q=term` and `POST /search` with the same query in the body, do the exact same lookup. Why might a team still prefer the GET version?
choices: GET's safety convention lets browsers/proxies cache and prefetch it, and it's bookmarkable and shareable as a plain URL — properties the equivalent POST doesn't get for free
POST is always meaningfully faster over the network
GET requests are structurally unable to carry query parameters
There's no real reason — they're identical in every practical way
items.explanation: Same result, different properties — GET's convention unlocks caching, prefetching, and shareability that a POST with an identical effect doesn't get automatically.

items.prompt: A junior engineer argues "DELETE and POST are basically the same, since both can remove data from a database via server code." What distinction is actually being missed?
choices: There is none — they're missing nothing real

DELETE's convention explicitly signals removal intent and (ideally) idempotence; a POST that happens to delete something as a side effect hides that intent from anything relying on the method name — same possible effect, very different signal to the rest of the system
POST can never physically delete anything at the network level
DELETE requests are defined to never have side effects
items.explanation: The method name is a signal other systems (caches, proxies, logs, retry logic) rely on — hiding a delete inside a POST throws that signal away even if the effect is the same.

items.prompt: Why does assigning the "wrong" method to a route (like a GET that deletes data) typically survive code review for a while before causing a real incident?
choices: Because it's actually a fine practice with no real risk

Because nothing in the running system enforces the convention — it keeps working right up until something that assumes GET is safe (a prefetcher, a crawler, a retry policy, a CDN) actually exercises that assumption
Because GET requests are blocked by the network from reaching delete handlers
Because this specific scenario is impossible to construct
items.explanation: A convention violation is invisible until something downstream that trusted the convention actually acts on it — that's usually what turns it into an incident.

items.prompt: An API gateway automatically retries any request that times out, for methods it considers "safe to repeat." items.prompt: Opening a browser's Network tab and viewing the "raw" request/response text shows something meaningfully real. Why, rather than it being a reconstruction?
choices: Because HTTP/1.1 messages genuinely are that exact text sent and received over the wire — there's no intermediate binary form being decoded purely for display
Because the browser always reconstructs a readable version purely for humans, differing from the real bytes
Because this trick only works in dev tools, not with tools like curl
Because HTTP removed text entirely, so this view is outdated
items.explanation: There's no decoding step here — the request/status line and headers you see are the literal bytes HTTP/1.1 sent.

items.prompt: A researcher intercepts unencrypted HTTP/1.1 traffic and reads the request in plain text with no special tools. What does this demonstrate about HTTP itself, separate from TLS?
choices: That HTTP without TLS is unusually buggy
That HTTP's message format is plain, human-readable text by design — TLS adds confidentiality on top, it doesn't change the underlying text format
That this specific researcher used an illegal method
That this is only possible using malware
items.explanation: TLS wraps the connection in encryption; it doesn't change what HTTP itself looks like underneath — which is readable text.

items.prompt: Could you, in principle, hand-write a valid HTTP/1.1 request with nothing but a text editor and a raw TCP tool, with zero HTTP-specific libraries?
choices: No — HTTP requires specialized binary-encoding tools
Yes — since HTTP/1.1 is correctly-formatted text over TCP, any tool that can open a TCP connection and send bytes can send one
No — only compiled HTTP clients can produce valid requests
Yes, but only for GET requests specifically
items.explanation: Nothing about HTTP/1.1's format requires a special library — it only requires sending the right text over the right connection.

items.prompt: Why does `curl -v` output look almost identical to what a browser's dev tools show for the same request, even though they're completely different programs?
choices: Pure coincidence between two unrelated tools
Because both are simply displaying the same underlying plain-text HTTP message — there's nothing proprietary to either tool about the message format itself
Because curl was built by copying browser internals directly
Because dev tools secretly invoke curl behind the scenes
items.explanation: Both tools are showing the same thing because the thing itself (the HTTP message) is the same plain text regardless of which tool sent it.

items.prompt: A new engineer assumes HTTP must have a hidden binary header before the readable part, "like most network protocols." What corrects that assumption, for HTTP/1.1?
choices: They're right — there is a hidden binary header

HTTP/1.1's message literally starts with the readable request/status line — no mandatory binary prefix precedes it; the assumption comes from protocols that do use binary framing, which HTTP/1.1 deliberately didn't
This is only true for responses, never for requests
This is only true when the connection uses HTTPS
items.explanation: HTTP/1.1 was deliberately designed as plain text from the very first byte — the assumption of a hidden binary header doesn't apply to it.

items.prompt: A support engineer debugs a production issue by SSH-ing into a box with no browser, no curl, and no HTTP library — only `nc` and a text editor. Why is this enough to fully diagnose an HTTP-level problem, and what's the one thing they still can't inspect this way if the traffic is HTTPS?

Because HTTP/1.1 is just text over TCP, they can hand-type a full request and read the raw response exactly as any client would — but over HTTPS they'd see encrypted bytes instead of the readable message, since nc doesn't perform TLS
This only works for inspecting responses, never requests

Displayed text never differs from the raw bytes, under any circumstance

The parser still sees headers "in progress" since there's no fully blank line yet — it may try to interpret the first body line as another header
The server automatically detects and fixes the missing blank line
The request is rejected with a specific "missing blank line" status code
items.explanation: Without the blank line, there's no signal that headers are finished — a correct parser keeps reading subsequent lines as more headers.

items.prompt: In a header-parsing loop that reads "one line at a time until a line is empty," what does "a line is empty" concretely mean at the byte level?

items.prompt: A parser bug reads headers correctly but then includes the leading blank line as part of the body, making every body one `\r\n` too long. What detail did the blank-line handling likely get wrong?

The bug is unrelated to the blank line at all

items.prompt: A half-written HTTP client library "forgets" to send the final blank line, yet appears to work during local testing against a very permissive test server. Why might it still fail against a real server?

Blank lines are optional in production HTTP servers
This kind of bug is impossible to actually write

This only matters for responses, never for requests

items.prompt: A server using `Connection: close` doesn't need to track message boundaries itself. Why not?
choices: The socket closing after one response IS the boundary signal — the parser can just read until EOF
Because close mode uses a special binary framing instead of text
Because keep-alive is actually required for any boundary detection to work
Because closing a connection never actually happens in HTTP/1.1
items.explanation: With `Connection: close`, EOF itself marks "this message is over" — there's nothing left to track.

items.prompt: Why can't a parser simply treat "one TCP `data` event" as "one request," even without pipelining?
choices: TCP may deliver a single request's bytes split across multiple `data` events — there's no reliable 1:1 mapping between network-level reads and application-level messages
Because `data` events are only ever emitted for responses, never requests
Because a request is always guaranteed to arrive in exactly one packet
This mapping actually is always reliable in practice
items.explanation: A `data` event is just however many bytes the OS happened to deliver right then — it has no obligation to align with message boundaries.

items.prompt: What's the risk of writing a keep-alive parser that assumes a request always arrives whole in one read, "because it usually does in local testing"?
choices: No risk — assuming a single clean read is always safe

Under real network conditions, large bodies or slow connections can split a request across multiple reads, so a parser relying on "always whole" will corrupt or hang on exactly the requests that don't fit the local testing conditions
There's no way to even test this locally, so the concern is moot
This risk only exists over HTTPS, never plain HTTP
items.explanation: Local testing over localhost tends to deliver everything in one clean read — production traffic over real networks won't cooperate the same way.

items.prompt: A pipelined connection delivers request 1 complete, plus the first half of request 2, in a single data event. What must a correct parser do with the leftover half-request bytes?
choices: Discard them — anything incomplete is malformed
Buffer them and wait for the rest to arrive in a subsequent data event before trying to parse request 2
Treat them as the start of a brand-new, unrelated connection
Immediately error out the entire connection
items.explanation: A correct parser keeps a buffer across reads specifically so a split message can be reassembled once the rest arrives.

items.prompt: Why does `Connection: close` make a parser's job strictly easier, at the cost of a new TCP handshake per request?
choices: Because the boundary problem keep-alive introduces simply doesn't exist under close — EOF is an unambiguous signal
Because close mode uses no headers at all
Because close mode is actually slower to parse than keep-alive
There's no real tradeoff — close is strictly better in every way
items.explanation: Close trades connection-reuse efficiency for a dead-simple boundary signal; keep-alive trades that simplicity for reused connections.

items.prompt: A proxy pools keep-alive connections to an upstream server and reuses them across unrelated client requests. A bug leaves leftover bytes from a previous, incompletely-consumed response body in the buffer when the connection is reused. What does the next request's parser likely do with those stale bytes, and why is this a serious bug class, not just a theoretical edge case?
choices: Nothing — stale bytes are automatically discarded on reuse

It will likely misinterpret the stale leftover bytes as the start of (or part of) a different exchange's response — this is exactly the shape of real response-smuggling / cross-request data-leakage bugs seen in production proxies, because connection reuse lets one request's incomplete parsing bleed into the next
The connection will always immediately and safely error out
This can only happen with chunked encoding, never with Content-Length
items.explanation: Connection reuse is exactly what turns an incomplete-parse bug into a cross-request leak — the next user's exchange inherits the previous one's leftover bytes.

items.prompt: Why is "wait for the connection to go idle, then assume the current message is complete" an unsafe strategy for detecting message boundaries under keep-alive, compared to tracking Content-Length or chunked encoding explicitly?
choices: It's not unsafe — idle time is a perfectly reliable signal

Network jitter or a slow client can make a connection momentarily idle mid-message with no relation to whether the message is actually complete — only the length-based signals the protocol actually provides are reliable
Idle detection is actually required by the HTTP/1.1 spec
This concern only matters for HTTP/2, not HTTP/1.1
items.explanation: Idle time measures the network, not the message — it has no defined relationship to "is this message done."

items.prompt: A client sends `PUT /settings` twice because of a doubled button click. Is this generally safe, and why?
choices: Yes — PUT is conventionally idempotent, so applying the same replacement twice should leave the same end state as applying it once
No — PUT always creates two separate resources
No — PUT carries the same retry-safety as POST
Yes, but only the first PUT is ever actually applied, which is a coincidence
items.explanation: Idempotency means the end state after two identical PUTs matches the end state after one — the double-click is harmless by convention.

items.prompt: Why is `POST /comments` NOT safe to blindly retry on a network timeout, even if the original request was perfectly well-formed?
choices: Because POST isn't conventionally idempotent — if the original request actually succeeded server-side before the timeout, a blind retry can create a second, duplicate comment
Because POST requests always fail on their second attempt
Because retries are blocked at the TCP layer specifically for POST
Because POST requests can't carry a body on a retry
items.explanation: A timeout doesn't tell you whether the first attempt actually failed or just failed to confirm — retrying a non-idempotent method risks duplicating a success you didn't hear back about.

items.prompt: A `GET /report?date=2024-01-01` request is retried 3 times by a flaky client. Why doesn't this risk creating 3 reports?
choices: GET is conventionally both safe (no side effects) and idempotent — a read-only lookup doesn't change state, so retrying it any number of times is harmless
GET requests are physically limited to one attempt per connection
The server automatically deduplicates requests by date
This actually does risk creating 3 separate reports
items.explanation: Nothing about a correctly-implemented GET changes state, so repeating it adds no risk regardless of how many times it's retried.

items.prompt: Why would a team design a `POST /payments` endpoint to accept a client-supplied `Idempotency-Key` header, given that POST itself isn't idempotent by convention?
choices: To let the client explicitly opt back into retry safety for an operation whose method doesn't grant it for free — the server can recognize a repeated key and return the original result instead of creating a duplicate
Idempotency keys have no actual effect on server behavior
This pattern only works for GET requests
This header is mandated by the HTTP spec for every POST endpoint
items.explanation: An idempotency key is the application layering retry-safety back onto a method that doesn't provide it by default — the same "build it on top" move statelessness uses for app state.

items.prompt: A junior engineer claims "since PUT is idempotent, it's always 100% safe to retry automatically, no exceptions." What's the gap in this claim?
choices: There's no gap — the claim is fully correct

Idempotency is a convention the server's own handler has to actually implement correctly — if the handler has a bug (like the earlier "deletes the next article" example), the method name alone doesn't guarantee the safe behavior
PUT requests can never be retried under any framework
Idempotent methods are rejected outright by every server on a second attempt
items.explanation: The method name is a promise, not an enforcement mechanism — a buggy handler can break the promise while the method is still technically "PUT."

items.prompt: A payment gateway's internal retry logic treats `POST /charge` as retry-safe because "it's just a POST, and our docs say POST timeouts are always safe to retry." The charge had actually succeeded before the client-visible timeout. What real-world failure does this produce, and what's the actual fix — not simply "don't retry at all"?

A duplicate charge to the customer; the fix isn't to avoid retries entirely (that sacrifices resilience to genuinely transient failures) but to make the *operation* idempotent via a client-supplied idempotency key the server deduplicates against, independent of the method's own convention
The client should switch the charge endpoint to GET instead
This isn't actually a real risk in production payment systems
items.explanation: The fix targets the operation's idempotency directly (a dedup key), rather than either trusting a false convention or giving up retries' resilience benefits entirely.

A handler bug (exactly like the earlier "deletes the next article" example) silently violates the convention — a blind retry policy with no verification of actual outcomes has no way to detect the violation until real damage has already accumulated
DELETE requests are physically prevented from ever being retried

Idempotency only ever applies to databases, never to logs or side systems
This gap can only occur with POST, never PUT

items.prompt: A client sends `Content-Length: 100` but then only sends 60 bytes before going silent. What is the server's parser left waiting for?
choices: It keeps waiting for the remaining 40 bytes the header promised, since nothing else signals the body is complete
It immediately assumes the body is done after 60 bytes
It automatically pads the missing bytes with zeros
It discards Content-Length entirely and starts the parse over
items.explanation: The header is a promise about the total body size — the parser has no reason to stop short of it on its own.

items.prompt: Why can't a receiver just "read until the connection goes idle" to find the end of a body, instead of trusting Content-Length?
choices: Idle time has no defined relationship to whether the full body has arrived — a slow network can go idle mid-body, and a fast one might never look idle before the next pipelined request's bytes arrive
Idle detection is actually the official HTTP boundary mechanism
Content-Length is optional, so idle detection is required as a fallback anyway
This concern only applies to HTTPS traffic
items.explanation: Idle time is a property of the network's timing, not of the message's actual length — the two have no reliable relationship.

items.prompt: A streamed response using chunked encoding sends a sequence of labeled chunks ending in a zero-length chunk. What is that zero-length chunk actually for?
choices: It's the explicit "body is complete" marker, replacing the role Content-Length plays when the full size isn't known upfront
It's an unrelated keep-alive ping
It signals that an error occurred mid-stream
It tells the client to restart the response from the beginning
items.explanation: Chunked encoding needs its own explicit end-of-body signal since there's no upfront total to count down from — the zero-length chunk is that signal.

items.prompt: Why would a server choose chunked encoding over Content-Length specifically for a live-generated CSV export?
choices: Because the full size of a report being generated on the fly isn't known until generation finishes, and chunked encoding lets the server start sending data immediately without computing the total size first
Because chunked encoding is always faster, regardless of use case
Because Content-Length doesn't function over HTTPS
Because CSV bodies are structurally incompatible with Content-Length
items.explanation: Chunked encoding exists precisely for the "I don't know the total size yet" case — a live export is a textbook example.

items.prompt: What specifically goes wrong if a server sends a Content-Length smaller than the body it actually writes?
choices: Nothing — extra bytes are simply ignored by every client
The receiver stops reading at the promised (too-short) length, treating the rest of the actual body as the start of a new, bogus message (or leftover garbage on a reused keep-alive connection)
The browser automatically detects and fixes the mismatched header
The server automatically catches and corrects this before sending
items.explanation: A receiver trusts the declared length completely — anything sent past it is no longer "this body," it's whatever comes next, misinterpreted.

items.prompt: A reverse proxy buffers a client's request body before forwarding it upstream, and recomputes `Content-Length` based on the bytes it actually buffered rather than trusting the client's original header. A request arrives with a body truncated mid-transfer (the client crashed), but the proxy's recomputed length matches the truncated bytes it received. What does this illustrate about trusting a *recomputed* length over catching the truncation itself?
choices: There's no real problem — recomputing the length always fixes any transfer issue

The proxy can make a truncated, incomplete request look "well-formed" to the upstream server simply by reporting however many bytes it actually got — silently passing along corrupted or incomplete data as if it were a complete, valid message
This specifically only happens with chunked encoding, never Content-Length
This behavior is a deliberate security feature, not a bug
items.explanation: Recomputing the length from what arrived doesn't validate that what arrived is actually complete — it just describes the truncated reality accurately, which is the problem.

Content-Length requires knowing the full size upfront; chunked encoding handles both the "size known upfront" case (as one big chunk) and the "size unknown until generation finishes" case — Content-Length alone can't represent the second case at all
Chunked encoding is actually less expressive than Content-Length
Content-Length can represent a streaming, size-unknown body just as well as chunked encoding

The health check hangs waiting for a socket close that a healthy keep-alive connection never provides — the health check's parser should have used Content-Length (or chunked framing) rather than assuming EOF-based framing that doesn't apply under keep-alive
The backend's configuration is definitely the one at fault here, not the health check
This can only happen with chunked encoding, never a fixed Content-Length

items.prompt: A client library automatically treats any `2xx` response as "the operation fully succeeded" without ever reading the body. What assumption is this library making, and where can it break?
choices: It assumes the status code and body always agree, which can break if the server's own logic sends a 200 while the operation it describes actually partially failed
This assumption is always safe and never breaks
It assumes the body is irrelevant to every possible use case by definition
It assumes 2xx responses are structurally forbidden from having a body
items.explanation: Status and body are independent fields set by the same server code — nothing enforces that the former accurately summarizes the latter.

items.prompt: Why would a well-designed API return `207 Multi-Status` for a batch operation where some items succeeded and others failed, instead of a single blanket `200`?
choices: Because a single status code can't represent "partially succeeded," so collapsing a mixed outcome into 200 would misrepresent what actually happened to any caller reading only the status
207 is required by every HTTP client library to function
200 is technically an invalid response for batch operations
There's no real reason — it's an arbitrary stylistic choice
items.explanation: A status code is a single claim — a genuinely mixed outcome needs a code (or a body) that actually says so, rather than rounding up to success.

items.prompt: A gateway in front of several microservices returns `200` for its own successful proxying, even when the downstream service it called actually returned a `500`. What's misleading about this gateway's behavior?
choices: Nothing is misleading — proxying success and downstream success are the same thing

It conflates "I successfully forwarded your request" with "the thing you asked for actually succeeded" — a caller reading only the gateway's status code sees 200 and reasonably assumes the operation worked
This configuration is physically impossible to build
500 responses can't pass through a gateway at all
items.explanation: Two different claims (did the proxy work vs. did the real operation work) got collapsed into one status code, hiding the one that actually matters to the caller.

items.prompt: Why is "trust the status code, skip body validation" a reasonable default for internal, well-tested services but a riskier one when integrating with a third-party API?
choices: It's equally risky (or equally safe) in both cases — trust level doesn't change anything

A third party's server-side discipline about honoring the status/body convention isn't something you control or have verified — the less you can vouch for a system's own correctness, the more a status-only check is really just trusting a stranger's word
Third-party APIs never return status codes at all
Internal services are contractually required to always be correct
items.explanation: Trusting a convention is reasonable when you've verified the other side actually honors it — with a third party, you usually haven't.

items.prompt: Team A's health check logs "healthy" for every 200 response, no matter what. Team B's logs "healthy" only when the response is 200 AND the body matches an expected shape. Which approach catches a bug where a crashed service's load balancer keeps returning a cached 200 from before the crash?
choices: Team A's — simplicity always wins

Team B's — the stale cached 200 is real evidence that the status claim can be present and still wrong; only checking the actual body content (freshness, shape) catches that the underlying system isn't what it claims
Neither — this scenario is impossible
Both equally, since they poll the same endpoint
items.explanation: This is exactly the opening scenario's lesson restated: the status alone can't distinguish "actually healthy" from "still claiming to be healthy."

items.prompt: An SRE argues for removing body validation from all alerts "to reduce alert noise," relying solely on status codes going forward. Using the Team A/Team B pattern from this unit's opening scenario, what's the concrete risk being traded away, and is there a middle ground?

The risk is reverting to Team A's multi-hour blind spot for exactly the failure mode (status claims success, reality doesn't) that body validation exists to catch; a middle ground is validating body *shape* cheaply (schema or size checks) rather than deep business-logic checks, keeping noise down without losing the core signal
The only fix is abandoning status codes entirely
Alert noise can only be solved by checking the body less, never more precisely
items.explanation: The tradeoff isn't "check the body or don't" — it's how deep that check goes, and a cheap shape check recovers most of the signal for little noise cost.

Status and body are actually always set by the exact same line of code
This observation has no practical design implications anywhere

Months later the origin starts returning errors, but the cache (only revalidating on an expiry) keeps serving the old, cached 200. From a "status code is a claim" lens, what is actually stale here — the claim, the evidence, or both?
choices: Neither — cached responses remain valid indefinitely by definition

Both — the cached response is a claim ("200, here's the body") frozen at the moment it was cached, and nothing about that claim updates just because reality (the origin's current state) has changed since; the claim was true when made and is now simply outdated, which is a distinct failure mode from "lying"
Only the body goes stale — the status code is timeless
This is purely a caching bug, unrelated to the claim/fact distinction
items.explanation: A claim can be perfectly honest at the moment it's made and still become wrong later — staleness is a different failure mode than dishonesty, and caching is exactly where it shows up.

items.prompt: A team adds a per-server rate limiter tracking "requests from this IP in the last minute" using in-memory counters on each server. What problem appears once there's more than one server behind a load balancer?
choices: None — rate limiting always works correctly regardless of server count

Each server only sees its own slice of that IP's requests, so the effective limit becomes (limit × number of servers) instead of the intended limit — the counters aren't shared across the now-interchangeable servers
This configuration breaks TLS termination
This is only a problem for GET requests
items.explanation: A limiter that lives on one server's memory silently stops being "the" limit once requests can land on any of several servers.

items.prompt: Why does a stateless API make it easier to add a second data center purely for redundancy, compared to an API with server-local session state?
choices: Stateless requests can be served correctly by any server in either data center — there's no session data tied to one specific server or location that needs replicating or routing around
A second data center always doubles throughput regardless of design
Statelessness automatically encrypts cross-datacenter traffic
Stateless APIs don't need a load balancer at all
items.explanation: Nothing has to be kept in sync between data centers if no server needs to remember a prior request to answer correctly.

items.prompt: A service's response to `GET /weather?city=austin` depends only on the request parameters, never on which server or data center answers it. What does this buy an operations team during a rolling deploy?
choices: Nothing special — rolling deploys work the same regardless of this property
Requests can be freely routed to whichever servers are already updated (or not) without worrying about a user's "session" being tied to one specific instance mid-rollout
Rolling deploys become entirely unnecessary
This only matters for POST requests
items.explanation: A rolling deploy mixes old and new instances temporarily — statelessness means it doesn't matter which one answers any given request.

items.prompt: Why is "the request alone determines the response" the precondition that makes HTTP caching possible at all, not just a nice-to-have?
choices: It's a nice optimization, but caching would work fine without it

If a response depended on hidden server-side memory instead of just the request, a cached copy from one moment couldn't be trusted to represent what a *different* moment's identical request would get back — caching assumes the request is the complete input
Caching has no relationship to this property whatsoever
This property is unrelated to GET requests specifically
items.explanation: A cache answers on the server's behalf — it can only do that safely if the request really is the whole story.

items.prompt: A monolith is split into independently stateless, horizontally scalable microservices. What single architectural property, carried over from HTTP's own statelessness, made this split tractable instead of requiring a session-coordination layer between the new services?
choices: TLS encryption between the services

The same "request alone determines the response" property, applied at the service level — each service can be scaled and routed to independently because no instance needs to remember a prior call to answer correctly
The monolith's original database schema
The specific programming language the services were rewritten in
items.explanation: Statelessness is the property that lets any instance of any service be substituted for any other — exactly what a clean service split needs.

items.prompt: A platform team is deciding whether a new internal service should be built stateless (horizontally scalable, no server affinity) or stateful (in-memory session cache, requires sticky routing) for a feature that genuinely needs very low-latency access to "the last 3 actions this user took." What's the actual tradeoff, framed honestly rather than "always go stateless"?
choices: There's no real tradeoff — stateless is strictly better in every case, no exceptions

Stateless costs a round-trip to a shared store (DB/cache) for that recent-actions lookup on every request, trading some latency and infrastructure for scaling simplicity and resilience to any single instance dying; a stateful, sticky-routed design can genuinely be faster for this access pattern but reintroduces the coordination and failover fragility statelessness was avoiding — the right call depends on how latency-critical this really is and how bad losing that in-memory state on a restart would be
Stateful designs are always faster with zero downside
This decision has no connection to HTTP's statelessness property at all
items.explanation: Real architecture tradeoffs rarely have a universally correct answer — the honest version names what's actually being traded, not just which side sounds more rigorous.

items.prompt: Why might an architecture review flag a new endpoint that reads from a request-scoped in-memory cache populated earlier in the *same* request's processing as a non-issue, while flagging a nearly identical-looking cache that persists *across* requests on the same server instance as a real statelessness violation?

A request-scoped cache lives and dies within a single request's handling — by the time the next request (from anyone) arrives, there's nothing left to depend on, so cross-request statelessness is untouched; a cache that survives across requests on one instance is exactly the server-local memory that breaks interchangeability between servers
Request-scoped caches are actually always worse for performance
This distinction only matters for GET requests
items.explanation: The lifetime of the cached state is the whole distinction — statelessness is a claim about what persists *between* requests, not about using memory *within* one.

items.prompt: Why should a client's parsing logic branch on the numeric status code rather than pattern-matching the reason phrase text?
choices: The reason phrase is a human-readable label with no guarantee of identical wording across servers, while the numeric code is the actual standardized, machine-meaningful field
Reason phrases are always empty strings in practice
The numeric code is slower to parse than text, but required anyway
Reason phrases are encrypted separately from the status code
items.explanation: The spec standardizes the number; it explicitly leaves the phrase free to vary — that asymmetry is the whole reason to key off the code.

items.prompt: A request line and a status line both have exactly three space-separated fields. Does this mean a parser could use the same field-splitting function for both?
choices: Yes — splitting on spaces to get three fields is mechanically identical for both; only what the caller does with each field afterward differs
No — request lines and status lines use entirely different delimiter characters
No — status lines actually have four fields, not three
Yes, and the interpretation of each field is identical too
items.explanation: The splitting step doesn't need to know or care what the fields mean — only the code that reads the result does.

items.prompt: In the request line `GET /articles/42 HTTP/1.1`, which field plays the same *structural position* as the status code `200` does in a status line?
choices: The method (GET) — it's the first field, mirroring the version's position in the status line
The path (/articles/42) — it sits in the second position, the same position the status code occupies in a status line
The HTTP version — it plays the same final role, but not the same position
There is no structural correspondence between any of the fields
items.explanation: Lining the two lines up field-by-field: method↔version, path↔status, version↔reason — the path and status code share the middle slot.

items.prompt: Why does "the status line's reason phrase can technically be any string" support the rule that clients shouldn't parse it?
choices: It doesn't support that rule at all
If the text is allowed to vary freely and isn't standardized, any logic depending on its exact wording is inherently fragile — which is exactly the argument for keying off the numeric code instead
This means status lines don't actually need a reason phrase
This means clients should parse the reason phrase even more carefully
items.explanation: An unconstrained field makes a poor foundation for logic that needs to be reliable across different servers.

items.prompt: Why would a log-parsing tool that extracts "the status" by regexing the first 3-digit number on the status line be more robust than one that tries to extract "success/failure" from the reason-phrase text?
choices: It wouldn't be more robust — text extraction is always more reliable
The numeric code is the standardized, position-stable field the protocol actually defines; reason-phrase text can vary by server, locale, or configuration in ways a fixed regex can't anticipate
Regexing numbers is slower, so this makes no practical difference
Reason phrases are actually guaranteed to be identical across every server
items.explanation: Same logic as the client case — a standardized field is a stable target for tooling in a way free-text never is.

A server is reconfigured to return `404` with a custom reason phrase of "Resource Missing" instead of the default "Not Found." What breaks, and what does this reveal about treating the reason phrase as meaningful?

The library will crash outright on any reconfigured phrase
This specific scenario violates the HTTP spec on the server's part
statusText is actually standardized to never be customized

items.prompt:
A buffer contains two complete, back-to-back pipelined requests: `"GET /a HTTP/1.1
Host: x

GET /b HTTP/1.1
Host: x

"`. Calling `findHeaderEnd` once on this buffer — what does it find, and what must the caller do to correctly discover the second request's boundary too?
choices: It finds both boundaries at once and returns an array

It finds only the *first* `\r\n\r\n` (the end of request #1's headers) — to find request #2's boundary, the caller must slice off everything up through and including that first boundary, then call `findHeaderEnd` again on the remaining buffer, repeating until no more boundaries are found (exactly the `while` loop pattern from L2/L3's keep-alive handling)
This buffer is malformed and findHeaderEnd would throw
The function automatically loops internally to find every boundary
items.explanation: `indexOf` only ever reports the first match — handling multiple pipelined messages is the caller's responsibility, via a loop that re-slices and re-searches.

Checking once per `data` event is sufficient and efficient as long as the check re-runs on *every* event (the buffer keeps growing until the boundary appears) — checking byte-by-byte would be wasteful (re-scanning on every single byte) without buying any earlier detection, since the boundary can only ever be found once all four of its characters have actually arrived

items.prompt: A team "fixes" CRLF injection by checking `if (value.includes("\r\n")) throw new Error(...)` instead of stripping `\r` and `\n` independently. What attack does this miss, and why?

A value containing a lone `

` together — many parsers (and some proxies that normalize line endings) treat a lone `
` or `` as a line break too, so this check has a gap the original sanitize-and-strip-both-independently approach doesn't

items.explanation: This is precisely the "common mistake" callout already in this topic's reference material — checking for the combined sequence instead of handling each character independently leaves a real gap.

Stripping silently changes the value the caller intended to send (which can produce a confusing but not dangerous result) while rejecting makes the problem visible immediately; for a public API, rejecting with a clear 4xx is often the safer default because silently mangling attacker-supplied input can still leave an unexpected, un-reviewed value in a header, even if the injection itself is blocked

items.prompt: A redirect handler builds `Location: ${userSuppliedUrl}` after running `userSuppliedUrl` through `sanitizeHeaderValue`. Does sanitizing for CRLF alone make this handler fully safe from URL-based attacks (like an open redirect to an attacker's phishing site)?
